transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, what brought me in today is that... I've been having this issue some evenings after work. Especially on days when I've been really strict with what I eat all day, I just end up eating way more than I ever meant to. 

I'll have my regular dinner, but then... I don't know, I just keep going. I'll have cereal, some crackers, whatever leftovers are sitting in the fridge, and then sweets. And it all happens within just a couple of hours. It's just getting to be a bit much, and I figured I needed to talk to someone about it.

After these episodes where you eat a lot more than you intended, do you do anything to try to compensate or undo what you've eaten? For example, do you make yourself vomit, use laxatives, exercise excessively, or restrict your eating the next day?

Well, I don't make myself throw up or take laxatives or anything like that. But... yeah, I guess I do try to make up for it. The next day, I'll usually just skip breakfast and lunch entirely. I tell myself it balances things out. Or I'll try to burn it off—like, I'll go for a really long hike, or when I'm at softball conditioning, I'll just push myself a lot harder than usual, even if I'm already exhausted. I just feel like I have to do something to undo it.

You mentioned you don't make yourself vomit or use laxatives. But I want to make sure I have the full picture—in a typical week, how many times would you say these binge episodes happen where you eat a lot in a short period of time?

Well, for the past few months, I'd say it's been happening most weeks. Usually, it's about one or two nights a week where I end up eating far more than I ever planned to. And then... yeah, the next day is when I try to make up for it by skipping my meals or exercising longer.

During these episodes when you're eating a lot—like the cereal, crackers, and sweets—do you feel like you have control over how much you're eating, or does it feel like you can't stop even if you wanted to?

I don't really feel like I have control, no. Once I get started on those nights... well, it's like I just keep going back to the kitchen. Even while I'm right there telling myself to stop, I just keep grabbing things. I don't really feel like I'm back in charge of what I'm doing until I'm just uncomfortably full.
During or right after these episodes when you're eating a lot, do you feel upset, guilty, or ashamed about what you're doing?

Yeah, definitely. I feel really guilty. Um... it's mostly just a lot of shame. While I'm doing it, I'm upset with myself, and then afterwards, I just feel terrible about the whole thing. It's a really bad feeling.
You mentioned these binge episodes have been happening for the past few months—can you tell me more specifically how long this pattern has been going on? Has it been at least 3 months?
Yes, it's been at least three months. It actually started right after my agency went through a big regional sales reorganization... so that was about four months ago.

I want to circle back on something—when you skip meals the next day or exercise harder, those are ways you try to make up for the binge. But I also want to ask directly: have you ever, even once or twice, made yourself vomit after one of these episodes, or is that something you've never done?
No, I've never done that. I know some people do, but making myself throw up... no, that's just not something I've ever tried. I just stick to the skipping meals and the exercise.

I want to make absolutely sure I understand this correctly—when you exercise harder the next day or skip meals, those are the only ways you try to compensate. But some people also use other methods like diet pills, diuretics, or enemas. Have you ever used any of those methods to try to counteract the binge eating?

No, I haven't. I've never taken any diet pills or anything like that. And I definitely haven't used diuretics or enemas. Like I said, it's really just the skipping meals and pushing myself harder at the gym. That's all I do.

When you have these binge episodes and then skip meals or exercise harder the next day, what are you most worried about? Are you primarily concerned about gaining weight or how your body looks, or is it more about just feeling like you need to 'undo' what you ate?

I think it's mostly about how I look, or... well, my weight. I get really worried about gaining weight. Like, if my waistband feels tight before a client luncheon or a big leadership meeting, I just start feeling like I look sloppy. And then I worry that people won't take me as seriously. I mean, I know I've still been doing my job well, but if my clothes don't fit right, I just feel like everyone is judging how I look. So I guess that's why I feel like I have to undo it.

You mentioned having one or two binge episodes per week, and then the next day you skip meals or exercise harder. On average, how many days per week would you say you're actually doing these compensatory behaviors—the skipping meals or the extra exercising?

Well, for the past few months, it's pretty much been happening most weeks. So if I have one or two nights where I eat way more than I meant to, then the next day is when I try to make up for it. I'd say I'm skipping meals or doing that extra exercise about one or two days a week, right after those bad nights.

When you think back over the past three months, on weeks when you have those binge episodes—would you say you're doing the skipping meals or extra exercising almost every single week, or are there some weeks where you have a binge night but don't do those compensatory things the next day?

Well, like I was just saying, for the past few months it really has been happening most weeks. Um... I don't really have times where I overeat and then just let it go. If I have one or two of those nights where I eat far more than I planned, I always try to make up for it the next day. So yeah, if the bad eating happens, the skipping meals or the longer workouts definitely happen right after.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (F50.81). Duration exceeds 3 months, meeting the minimum threshold.
